source.title: A Resizable Mini-batch Gradient Descent based on a Randomized Weighted Majority
source.authors: S. Cho; Sunghun Kang; C. Yoo

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the paper through its conclusion and references; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares test accuracy across fixed mini-batch sizes under fixed epoch counts on MNIST and CIFAR10, testing batch-size effects with its own settings and measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior work on large-batch generalization, but those cited results are not rows. Rows below record the paper's own fixed-batch test-accuracy results. The RMGD results concern its adaptive method and are not rows for the fixed-batch claim.
record.test_reason: The study's own fixed-batch comparisons measure held-out accuracy under equal epoch budgets, directly testing V5. MNIST uses fixed learning rates; CIFAR10 scales learning rate with batch size. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the authors: batch-size choice affects accuracy and efficiency, and RMGD achieves or exceeds the best fixed-batch mean with much less time than exhaustive grid search. Their claimed high probability should remain attributed to them: a p-value of 0.155 does not establish an 84.5% probability of matching grid-search performance.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares fixed MGD batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets and also proposes adaptive batch-size selection; it does not reproduce the cited large-batch studies' full recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: The relative test accuracy by batch size differs between MNIST and CIFAR10; on MNIST the optimizer also accompanies different batch-size patterns.
record.problems: The study reports test accuracy, not training error or the training-to-test gap. It compares batch sizes on only two image datasets and does not report a broad sweep of batch size beyond a specified workload-dependent threshold.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying fixed-batch test-accuracy rows were left out. Adaptive RMGD and aggregate grid-search rows were excluded because they do not report outcomes for a fixed batch-size condition.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width dependence beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and learned local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning.

Language models; identification of the workload-dependent batch threshold; batches above 512 on MNIST or 256 on CIFAR10; longer-training remedies; warmup; controlled comparisons isolating learning-rate scaling or normalization and regularization changes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout; dropout is present in CIFAR10 without an ablation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its association with generalization gaps.
Removing memorized training examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All recorded accuracy values and standard deviations match the tables. MNIST conditions have 100 repetitions and CIFAR10 conditions 25. Table 5 tests RMGD against fixed-batch methods, not differences among fixed batch sizes. CIFAR10 results qualify scope rather than challenge V5, which already allows recipe-dependent exceptions and a workload-dependent threshold. Declared omissions of RMGD method-performance rows are appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Language models; larger batches beyond the workload-dependent threshold; longer training and recipe changes such as warmup, normalization, or regularization.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the generalization gap.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.

relationships.condition: MNIST CNN, Adam, fixed learning rate 0.0001, 100 epochs
relationships.reason: r1–r6 show lower mean accuracy at batches 128–512 than at 16–64; batch 512 reaches 99.254% versus 99.328% at 64.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest lower mean Adam accuracy at the larger batches. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: MNIST CNN, Adagrad, fixed learning rate 0.1, 100 epochs
relationships.reason: r7–r12 show batches 256–512 below all batches 16–128; batch 512 reaches 99.198% versus 99.277% at 64. V5 does not require monotonic decline at smaller batches.
relationships.display_finding: The study's results suggest the largest Adagrad batches underperformed the smaller batches without a monotonic trend throughout. These results have not been verified.

relationships.condition: CIFAR10 All-CNN-C, momentum, batch-proportional learning rates, dropout and weight decay, 350 epochs
relationships.reason: r13–r17 show no mean accuracy penalty through batch 256: 87.897% versus 87.778% at 16. The adapted recipe and unidentified threshold limit inference about larger batches.
relationships.display_finding: The study reports no mean accuracy penalty across the tested batches under the adapted recipe, but these comparisons remain unverified and the threshold for larger batches was undetermined.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: Smaller batch sizes 16–64 have higher mean test accuracy than 256–512 (r1–r3, r5–r6). The paper describes relatively small batches as higher-performing on MNIST.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Accuracy does not decline monotonically with batch size: batch sizes 32–128 exceed batch size 16, while the largest sizes perform worse (r7–r12).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports larger batches 128–256 outperforming 16–64; batch size 256 has the highest mean accuracy (r13–r17).
